From: Lena Brooks <lena.brooks@harbor-coverage.example>
To: Morgan Ibarra <morgan.ibarra@northline.example>
Cc: Dana Okonkwo <dana.okonkwo@northline.example>, Ruth Alvarez <ruth.alvarez@harbor-coverage.example>
Date: Tuesday, 1 December 2026, 10:20 America/Los_Angeles
Subject: What Harbor promises the desk

Morgan,

I am Lena Brooks, Harbor Coverage supervisor, Seattle. I am writing on Tuesday, 1 December 2026, an office day. The correspondence unit works Monday through Friday. Saturday and Sunday are not days this unit issues a new answer. I am writing to you as desk supervisor at the Vancouver desk of Northline Access Collaborative, and I am copying Dana Okonkwo because the ask I am answering has come through your office with her name on the need for a shorter sentence. Ruth Alvarez is copied because she records the rows and will not be told, by anyone, to rewrite one.

This letter is what Harbor promises the desk.

Harbor promises one of three answers. The words are yes, no, and timeout. They are different answers. The desk receives the word that was recorded. The desk does not receive a fourth word, and the desk does not receive permission to treat one of the three as if it were another.

A yes is the word yes on the row. When that row has a window, the window stays with the yes. A yes is the promise only as the row wrote it, word and dates together when the dates are on the row. I am not, in this letter, naming a window for a particular member. I am naming the shape of the promise.

A no is the word no on the row. A no is not a yes that the clerk ran out of time to finish. A no is not a timeout. If the row says no, the promise to the desk is no.

A timeout is the third answer. The check did not come back yes, and it did not come back no. The line did not answer. The clerk writes timeout. A timeout has no window. There is no start, no end, and no count of days for the desk to pencil in. The promise, when the row says timeout, is the word timeout.

A timeout is not a grant. I want that sentence on its own, because your office has been asking me to treat it as one. A timeout is not permission to tell a member they may proceed. A timeout is not permission to tell a member the request was granted and the paperwork will catch up. A timeout is not a yes with the dates left blank. A timeout is not a quiet grant that the counter may use while the word timeout sits in a footnote. There is no grant inside it. The answer is the word on the row.

A missing reply is a different event from a timeout, and it is also not a grant. The standing footnote on our correspondence says a missing reply is not a grant. I am not withdrawing that footnote. A timeout is a word we did record. A missing reply is a reply we did not send. The desk has tried, in conversation, to use the difference as a hinge: if a missing reply is not a grant, perhaps a recorded timeout is close enough to one. It is not. A timeout is not a grant. A missing reply is not a grant. I will not bend either sentence into permission.

I am noting the ask in this letter so it is not only in the hallway. The Vancouver desk has asked me to bend the promise. You have asked that a timeout be usable at the counter as a grant, so a member is not left with a blank and a clerk is not left with a word the member cannot travel on. Dana has asked, through you, for a shorter sentence the counter can say. I have heard the ask. I have not agreed. I do not agree in this letter. I will not instruct Ruth to rewrite a timeout into a grant, into a yes, or into a window.

This letter does not name a clock for a screen. It says what Harbor promises the desk: yes, no, or timeout. A timeout is not a grant.

Lena Brooks
Supervisor
Harbor Coverage
Seattle

From: Morgan Ibarra <morgan.ibarra@northline.example>
To: Lena Brooks <lena.brooks@harbor-coverage.example>
Cc: Dana Okonkwo <dana.okonkwo@northline.example>
Date: Tuesday, 1 December 2026, 13:10 America/Vancouver
Subject: Re: What Harbor promises the desk

Lena,

I am Morgan Ibarra, desk supervisor, Vancouver. Thank you for the three words in writing. I am asking again, on the same day, and I am asking in mail so the ask is as visible as the refusal.

The counter meets timeouts. When the row says timeout, the clerks have a word and no window, and the member still asks what they are allowed to do next. I have asked you to bend the promise far enough that a timeout can be read as a grant of time: the member stays in the queue, the desk does not invent a yes, and the member is not told to go home as if Harbor had refused them. I have also asked, when Dana has needed a sentence for the floor, whether a timeout can be read as a grant to proceed to the clinic and sort the coverage row afterward. I am putting both versions of the ask in this note. They are both asks. I am not announcing either one as the practice of this desk.

I have not told a member they are covered on the strength of a timeout. I have not told a clerk to pencil dates onto an empty window. What I am asking is whether Harbor's promise can flex, for the counter, so that timeout is not a dead stop. If the answer is that it cannot flex, I need that as your answer, not as my guess. The office week here is Monday through Friday, the same shape as yours. I am asking on a Tuesday, inside the week.

I understand you to have written that you have not agreed. I am asking you to look at the bend one more time before the day ends. A grant of time, with no yes and no dates, is the smallest bend I know how to describe. If even that is a grant you will not give, say so.

Morgan Ibarra
Desk supervisor
Northline Access Collaborative
Vancouver desk

From: Lena Brooks <lena.brooks@harbor-coverage.example>
To: Morgan Ibarra <morgan.ibarra@northline.example>
Cc: Dana Okonkwo <dana.okonkwo@northline.example>, Ruth Alvarez <ruth.alvarez@harbor-coverage.example>
Date: Tuesday, 1 December 2026, 15:05 America/Los_Angeles
Subject: Re: What Harbor promises the desk

Morgan,

I looked again. I have not agreed.

A grant of time is still a grant. You described it as the smallest bend: the member stays in the queue, the desk does not invent a yes, and nobody pencils a window. The smallest bend is still a bend. Harbor's promise to the desk is yes, no, or timeout. A timeout is not a grant, including a grant of time to proceed, a grant of time to remain as if something had been allowed, or a grant to go to a clinic and sort the row later. Going to a clinic on a timeout, with the row still timeout, would be the member traveling on a permission I did not record.

I am not adding a fourth promise. "Timeout, but you may proceed" is a fourth promise. "Timeout, but the queue itself is the grant" is a fourth promise. I will not write either of them into the unit, and I will not tell Ruth Alvarez to write them on a row. Ruth records yes, no, or timeout. A timeout stays timeout. It has no window. It is not a grant.

The desk has asked me to bend this. You have asked twice in substance, the hallway version and today's mail, and the mail now includes both the grant of time and the grant to proceed. Dana's need for a shorter counter sentence is part of the same ask. I have not agreed. This afternoon's letter is the same position as this morning's letter. I am not softening it because you made the bend sound small.

A missing reply remains not a grant. A timeout remains not a grant. Use the word that is on the row. If the word is timeout, the word you have for the member is timeout. I am not supplying a travel sentence to go with it.

Lena Brooks
Supervisor
Harbor Coverage
Seattle

Lena,

I am Dana Okonkwo, operations director at the Vancouver desk. Morgan told me he had asked you to bend the promise, and I have now read both of your letters and his. I want the director's copy to be explicit.

I am not instructing you, in this note, to bend it. I am asking you to confirm, to me, the promise as it stands after the ask. The floor will hear a rumor that a supervisor asked and that a director wanted a shorter sentence, and the rumor will try to become the practice. From: Lena Brooks <lena.brooks@harbor-coverage.example>
To: Dana Okonkwo <dana.okonkwo@northline.example>

Date: Tuesday, 1 December 2026, 17:10 America/Los_Angeles
Subject: Re: What Harbor promises the desk

Dana,

The promise stands, after the ask, as it stood before the ask.

What Harbor promises the desk is one of three answers: yes, no, or timeout. A yes is yes, with the window when the row has a window. A no is no. A timeout is timeout. A timeout has no window. A timeout is not a grant. A missing reply is not a grant either, and that footnote is still standing. Neither sentence has been bent into permission for the counter.

The desk has asked me to bend it. Morgan asked that a timeout be usable as a grant of time, and he asked that it be usable as a grant to proceed to a clinic and sort the row afterward. He wrote that you have needed a shorter sentence for the floor. I am noting the ask so your copy has it from me, not only from hallway memory. I have not agreed. I did not agree this morning. I did not agree this afternoon. I do not agree in this letter to you.

Ruth Alvarez will keep recording yes, no, or timeout. I am not instructing her to add a travel sentence, a blank window, or a grant beside a timeout. The Vancouver desk may tell a member the word that is on the row. The desk may not tell the member that a timeout granted the request. I am not naming a clock for a screen in this letter. I am naming the promise.

You may keep this page. It is the page I will still mean when the next ask arrives. The next ask will get the same answer unless I write a different one. I have not written a different one. Harbor promises the desk yes, no, or timeout. A timeout is not a grant. The desk has asked me to bend that. I have not agreed.

Lena Brooks
Supervisor
Harbor Coverage
Seattle
